Newborn Care

Using an infant swing while your baby is awake

Updated: November 16, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

You set your baby in a swing while you sit nearby with lunch. Their eyelids start to close. That is the moment to take them out and put them on their back in their usual safe sleep space. Planning where you will move them makes that small decision easier, especially when you are tired yourself.

Before you put your baby in the seat

An indoor infant swing is optional equipment for short periods when the baby is awake and a caregiver is watching. Read the instructions for the exact model, including its minimum size, weight limit, allowed recline settings and developmental stopping point. Check the model number for recalls, especially for a borrowed or second-hand swing. Leave it unused if the harness, fastenings or instructions are missing until you can verify and correct the problem.

Stand the swing on a firm, level floor. Keep it off counters, tables and beds. Fasten every part of the supplied restraint snugly as directed, even for a short turn. For a young baby, follow the required recline setting so their head does not slump forward. Keep the face visible and free. Do not add pillows, blankets for propping or an insert that the manufacturer has not approved.

When the baby dozes

A seated baby with limited head control can slump so that their chin presses toward their chest and breathing becomes difficult. A harness helps prevent a fall, but cannot turn an inclined swing into a safe sleep surface. Watching the swing or stopping its movement does not make it suitable for a nap.

As soon as you notice your baby falling asleep, transfer them to a crib, bassinet or other approved infant sleep space. Place them on their back on a firm, flat, level mattress with a fitted sheet and no loose bedding or soft objects. Use that arrangement for naps as well as night sleep. If your baby is struggling to breathe, looks blue or is unresponsive, call emergency services immediately.

What the seating study actually counted

A review of 11,779 sleep-related infant deaths recorded 348 in sitting devices. That category included car seats, swings and other seats, and most of the 348 occurred in car seats. The researchers reviewed deaths, without counting every time a baby used a seat. Those figures cannot tell a family the risk of a single swing session or how many deaths were caused by a particular swing.

You can act on what is known without calculating a risk. Show anyone looking after your baby where the empty crib is and agree that if the baby dozes in the swing, that person will move them. Put the baby in the crib if you are about to step away, become distracted or fall asleep yourself.

Give the baby other places to move

Time in seats keeps pressure on the back of the head and limits opportunities to turn, reach and move freely. Alternate holding your baby with supervised play on the floor, including short periods of tummy time while awake. Keep placing the baby on their back for sleep. If they always turn the same way or you notice flattening, ask the clinician to check head shape and neck movement.

Stop using the swing at the first limit your model lists, whether it is weight, size or a new ability such as attempting to climb out. Some designs have earlier rolling or pushing-up limits. A child’s birthday by itself will not tell you when the seat is suitable or when it has been outgrown.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Use the complete harness on a stable floor and follow the specific model’s instructions.

Transfer a drowsy or sleeping baby to a clear, firm, flat, level sleep surface on their back.

Offer supervised tummy time only while awake.

How BeMama can help

BeMama suggests showing every caregiver the place where the baby will sleep before the swing is used for the first time.

When to seek help

Remove a baby whose head slumps forward. If the baby has difficulty breathing, turns blue or is unresponsive, call emergency services immediately. Move any sleeping baby to the approved sleep space.

Sources and further reading

  • American Academy of Pediatrics — Recommendations for a safe infant sleep environment
  • Liaw and colleagues, Pediatrics — Sleep-related infant deaths in sitting devices
  • US Consumer Product Safety Commission — Safety requirements and warnings for infant swings

Links lead directly to guidance from the organizations named above.

Evidence notes updated: November 16, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Check the model, recall status, size limits and complete restraints before using a swing.
  • Supervise awake use and move a sleeping baby onto their back on a firm, flat sleep surface.
  • Offer awake floor play and stop using the swing when the first manufacturer limit is reached.

Frequently asked questions

At what age can I put a baby in a swing?

Use the instructions for your exact model. Check minimum size, the recline setting for a young baby and the developmental and weight limits. A seat that does not fit or cannot keep the head well positioned is unsuitable.

What should I check each time?

Place the swing on the floor, secure the complete harness, see that the baby’s head and face are clear and stay nearby watching. Have an empty safe sleep space ready if the baby dozes.

Can a swing cause a flat spot on a baby’s head?

Long periods resting in one position can contribute to flattening. Give your baby opportunities to move on the floor and have supervised awake tummy time. Use the back for sleep, and ask about persistent flattening or a head-turn preference.

Do we need to buy an infant swing?

No. It can be an option for brief supervised awake use in a correctly fitted seat. A safe place on the floor for awake play and a separate approved sleep space meet different needs without a swing.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
